title: Google Discover To Undergo Dramatic Changes via @sejournal, @martinibuster
content:
A new job posting for a Principal UX Lead for Discover, appears to indicate that Google is planning a substantial transformation of Discover, their recommendation engine for articles. The posting strongly suggests that Google plans to overhaul Discover into an AI-powered experience to become more deeply personalized.
The job posting shows that Google may be planning to change Discover into an AI-powered experience that anticipates users’ interests, helps them accomplish goals, and connects them with content and services across Google’s ecosystem. It describes a Discover that more interactive, deeply personalized, and more competitive with social media feeds. It’s possible that some of the changes are already being tested because I recently experienced suggestions for Meta Threads in Discover.
If these changes come to pass, this may mean a change to how publishers and creators reach audiences through Discover because what’s described is more than an effort to improve content recommendations. Google is describing a different purpose for Discover that leans more toward helping users act on information.
One of the most consequential changes to Discover is the re-conceptualization of it from a recommendation engine to a concierge. A concierge is a person that arranges services and obtains things on behalf of another person.
“Lead the design vision and execution to transform Discover into a proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience that helps users make progress on their goals.”
The phrase “proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience” suggests Google wants Discover to anticipate what users need rather than simply recommend articles based on past search patterns that indicate user interests.
What that means is that instead of recommending articles about a topic, Discover could recognize an ongoing interest or goal and recommend information, products, services, and next steps for accomplishing the task that’s inherent in the interest.
This is a strong match for how Google’s CEO Sundar Pichai envisions the future of search, what he refers to as Agentic Search that fits within a task-based paradigm.
“I feel like in search, with every shift, you’re able to do more with it. …If I fast forward, a lot of what are just information seeking queries will be agentic search. You will be completing tasks, you have many threads running.”
The full job posting for that section outlines the direction Google Discover is taking:
“Lead the design vision and execution to transform Discover into a proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience that helps users make progress on their goals.
Balance AI capabilities while centering human voices and sources.
Develop thoughtful, user-first strategies for making Discover a more impact experience that serves a scaled consumer base and helps existing users go deeper, moving seamlessly from inspiration to action.”
The phrases “concierge experience,” “make progress on their goals,” and “inspiration to action” describe a radical change away from how Google Discover’s current function as a recommendation engine.
A 2026 Google research paper describes a recommender system that identifies a user’s semantic intent, particularly for understanding soft attributes, which are highly subjective and personalized.
One thing that won’t change with Discover is that it will still mine user interaction data, but that how that data is interpreted will be redefined.
“You will lead strategic design initiatives to redefine feed interactions, content formats, and AI-driven exploration experiences.”
Another clue is that Google intends to innovate new feed formats with AI that are focused on engagement but also with showing more human creators, which should be good for publishers.
“Evolve feed formats by scaling AI enabled formats, designing new engagement mechanisms, and elevating human voices and perspectives in the feed.”
Discover is currently tightly associated with Search, as some of the hints about what users are interested are derived from their search patterns. That’s probably why Discover is considered a subset of Search in Google Search Console.
The job posting indicates that the person hired must be able to work together with other parts of Google, including YouTube.
“You will partner closely with executive leadership across Product Management, Engineering, Data Science, UX Research, and cross-organization partners (YouTube, Shopping, Chrome, and Android) to deliver a unified experience.”
Another interesting takeaway is how they will be targeting youth. The posting didn’t indicate how young this targeting will reach.
“Proven track record of defining product strategy for youth demographics and driving product-market fit in competitive content ecosystems.”
That phrase “product-market fit” is a reference to how well a product meets the expectations of the demographic it was designed for.
The insight here is that Google is looking for a person who can make Discover more attractive and younger audiences and increase engagement and stickiness.
Hat tip to @AndellDam for spotting the job posting and sharing it on X.

title: Your social media following isn’t the asset you think it is
content:
Imagine your company has 50,000 followers on LinkedIn. You’ve spent years building that audience. You publish useful content. People follow you because they want to hear what you have to say. It feels like an asset because it is.
You own the content you create. You control your company’s LinkedIn account within the platform’s rules. But you don’t control whether those 50,000 followers see your next post. LinkedIn does.
Having access to an audience isn’t the same as having a direct relationship with it.
Many marketers are familiar with the PESO model: paid, earned, shared, and owned media. Gini Dietrich introduced the model in 2014 as a way to think more holistically about how these different types of media work together.
Social media falls primarily into the shared category. Your website and blog are owned. Media coverage is earned. Advertising is paid.
It’s a useful framework. But I think marketers need to add another question: Who controls your access to the audience?
You can own your website and publish an article there. But if you depend on LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, X, or another third-party platform to drive traffic to that article, you don’t control the connection between your content and the people you want to reach. The platform does.
The world’s most powerful SEO platform, purpose-built for Enterprise.
MySpace is an extreme example. At its peak, it was the dominant U.S. social network. Then its audience moved elsewhere. Brands that had spent years building followings there couldn’t take those followers with them.
Twitter/X offers a different lesson. After Elon Musk acquired the company in 2022, policies, features, and user behavior changed rapidly. Advertisers reconsidered their participation. Eventually, even the name changed. Brands didn’t control any of those decisions.
But it doesn’t take the decline of a dominant platform or a change in ownership to disrupt your access to an audience. An algorithm change will do.
A B2B company I previously worked with publishes strong thought-leadership content on its blog.
When a new article is published, there’s a concerted effort to promote it through social media. LinkedIn is the primary platform, with X and Instagram playing supporting roles. But traffic from those efforts isn’t what it once was.
The company has responded in part by bringing in outside industry experts as contributors — their names and networks help extend the reach of its content. It’s helped, but it hasn’t solved the underlying problem.
The company doesn’t have an email newsletter. It doesn’t do email marketing at all. This is a complex B2B sale that typically requires a salesperson, so prospects do receive emails from individual salespeople. But those are ad hoc, one-to-one communications.
What strikes me is that they’re essentially starting from zero with every new article. They work to get people to the content, but there’s no systematic next step for someone who likes what they find to say, “I’d like to hear more from you.”
When the next article publishes, the company has to go out and find an audience all over again.
We talked about email marketing. The concern is resources. Building an email program takes time and money, and both are limited. But the company is already investing resources in creating content and finding new ways to attract people to it.
What it’s not investing in is turning that attention into an ongoing relationship.
Platform news, strategy analysis, and industry trends. Trusted by 40,000+ marketing professionals.
None of this means companies should abandon social media. Quite the opposite. One of the things I tell my Georgetown University digital marketing students is:
Be where your people are. Be useful when you get there.
Social media can be very good at providing a low-commitment way for someone to get to know you. They can watch a video, read a post, click through to an article, or follow you. They can engage with something you publish or simply lurk for six months.
That’s valuable. You’re earning their attention and, hopefully, their trust. But once someone has decided that what you provide is valuable, give them an opportunity to take the relationship further.
That might mean subscribing to a newsletter, registering for an event, downloading useful content, signing up for SMS, or creating an account. The specific next step will depend on your business and your audience. What matters is that you’re creating a way for someone to say, “Yes, I’d like to hear from you again.”
The objective isn’t to get people off social media. It’s to stop making social media the only way you can reach them.
Email changes the equation because it’s a direct route to the audience. You don’t need an algorithm to show your post, a publisher to cover you, or a search engine to surface your content.
But here’s where I want to be careful with the word “own.” Getting someone’s email address doesn’t mean you own the audience. They’ve given you permission to contact them, and that permission isn’t unlimited. It can also be withdrawn at any time.
Which brings us back to what marketers should actually be trying to build: relationships.
I tell my students that the email address isn’t the most valuable thing. The willingness of the person behind it to keep paying attention is. That’s the asset.
Social media can help you earn that attention. Email, SMS, and other direct channels can help you maintain it. But no channel gives you ownership of an audience. The relationship only lasts as long as you’re giving people a reason to continue it.
When you’ve built that relationship, the next time you have something worth saying, you don’t have to start from zero.
Author’s note: I developed the core argument and provided the client example and teaching materials that informed this article. I collaborated with ChatGPT to research and fact-check the historical examples, pressure-test and organize my thinking, and assist with outlining and drafting. I reviewed, revised, and approved the final article.
